En 1951 <strong>Claude Shannon</strong>: In 1951 Claude Shannon published a lovely experiment to measure the entropy of English: he gave a person a cut-off text and asked them to guess the next letter, noting how many attempts they needed. From those figures he deduced that each letter of English carries approximately one bit of information, far less than the 4.7 bits that would be needed if the twenty-six letters were equally likely. That paper, Prediction and Entropy of Printed English, is perplexity's direct ancestor: measuring a language model is exactly repeating Shannon's experiment with a machine instead of a person.
